positions/feminist-womanist-theology/one: Women’s experience is a neglected source and test of theology: patriarchal readings and images of God must be critiqued, and the liberating, egalitarian strands of Scripture and tradition recovered, with Black, Latina and African women naming their own distinct experiences.
positions/feminist-womanist-theology/cor: Women and men are equally the image of God (Genesis 1:27) and one in Christ (Galatians 3:28).
Whatever diminishes the full humanity of women is not redemptive (Ruether).
Exclusive male language for God and male-only leadership reflect culture more than revelation.
Womanist theology (Williams, Grant, Cannon) centres Black women’s survival; African women’s theology (Oduyoye) addresses culture and church.
positions/feminist-womanist-theology/ori: Grew from the 1960s women’s movement (Valerie Saiving’s 1960 essay; Mary Daly 1968) into systematic work by Rosemary Radford Ruether, Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Elizabeth Johnson; womanist theology from Delores Williams, Jacquelyn Grant and Katie Cannon (1980s-90s); the Circle of Concerned African Women Theologians from 1989.
positions/feminist-womanist-theology/str: It recovers women’s voices and roles in Scripture and church history.
It exposes ways theology has justified domination.
Womanist and global voices ensure that "women’s experience" is not universalised from white Western women.
Traditionalists argue it subordinates revelation to experience and changes the names of God given by Christ.
Some critics see radical forms (e.g. post-Christian feminism) as leaving Christianity behind.
Womanist critics charged early feminism with racial blindness.
positions/feminist-womanist-theology/res: Many feminist theologians remain within orthodox frameworks, arguing that critique serves faithfulness; evangelical egalitarians make similar exegetical arguments.
positions/feminist-womanist-theology/con: Debates over women’s ordination and inclusive language.
New readings of Scripture and history.
positions/african-theology/oneLine: God was already known and at work in Africa before missionaries; the gospel must be expressed in African languages, cultures and religious categories, as the early Church expressed it in Greek ones.
positions/african-theology/coreClaims/0: African traditional religion is a preparation for the gospel (praeparatio evangelica).
positions/african-theology/coreClaims/1: Mother-tongue Scripture makes Christianity a non-Western religion in Africa (Sanneh, Bediako).
positions/african-theology/coreClaims/2: Ancestors, community, healing and the spirit world are theological questions, not superstitions to be ignored.
positions/african-theology/coreClaims/3: African Christianity continues the early African church of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine.
positions/african-theology/origin: Began with Des prêtres noirs s’interrogent (1956), by francophone Catholic priests, and with the Ecumenical Association of African Theologians (1977); shaped by John Mbiti, Bolaji Idowu, Harry Sawyerr, Kwame Bediako, Mercy Amba Oduyoye, Jean-Marc Éla and Lamin Sanneh, and expressed in African Independent and Pentecostal churches.
positions/african-theology/strongestArgu: It makes Christianity at home in Africa rather than a foreign import.
It draws on the reality that Africa is now a demographic centre of world Christianity.
It recovers neglected biblical themes (the spirit world, community, healing).
positions/african-theology/strongestObje: Evangelicals such as Byang Kato warned of syncretism and universalism.
Liberation-oriented African theologians said inculturation neglected poverty and politics.
Some argue it idealises a single "African" worldview across diverse cultures.
positions/african-theology/responses/0: Bediako argued that Christ is the fulfilment, not the negation, of the African past, and that all theology is culturally embedded.
positions/african-theology/consequences/: Liturgical inculturation (e.g. the Zaire Use of the Roman Rite, 1988).
Academic centres such as Akrofi-Christaller Institute.
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/na: Asian contextual theologies (minjung, Dalit and others)
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/al: Theology of the pain of God
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/on: Christian theology in Asia must speak from Asia’s religious plurality, its poverty and its suffering peoples, using Asian stories and categories rather than imported Western systems.
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/co: God is revealed among the suffering: the minjung (Korea) and the Dalits (India) are subjects of theology.
Asian religious traditions and stories are conversation partners for theology.
The pain or compassion of God is central (Kitamori, Song).
Theology begins with the neighbour and the concrete situation (Koyama).
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/ke: Kitamori, Theology of the Pain of God (1946)
Ahn Byung-mu, Jesus and the Minjung (1977)
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/or: Pioneered by Kazoh Kitamori in Japan (1946), M. M. Thomas in India, Kosuke Koyama and C. S. Song (1970s), Korean minjung theologians under dictatorship (1970s) and Dalit theologians such as Arvind Nirmal (1980s); Aloysius Pieris in Sri Lanka joined liberation and Buddhist dialogue.
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/st: It makes theology answerable to Asia’s majority poor and to its ancient religious cultures.
It recovers biblical solidarity with the suffering.
It enriches global theology with new images (the pain of God, han, waterbuffalo).
Asian evangelicals and Pentecostals, who are numerically far stronger, often regard it as elite and syncretistic.
Critics say minjung theology risked identifying a social class with Christ.
Others note that Asian Christians in persecuted churches prefer traditional doctrine.
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/re: Contextual theologians respond that all theology is contextual and that solidarity with sufferers is biblical.
positions/asian-contextual-theologies/co: Influence on Asian ecumenical bodies (Christian Conference of Asia).
positions/pentecostal-theology/oneLine: Theology should be shaped by the experience of the Spirit poured out on all flesh: a "full gospel" of Jesus as Saviour, Sanctifier, Spirit-baptiser, Healer and coming King, articulated through testimony, worship and mission.
positions/pentecostal-theology/coreClaim: The Spirit’s experiential presence (tongues, healing, prophecy) is normal Christianity.
Theology is done in worship, testimony and mission as much as in study (orthopathy with orthodoxy and orthopraxy).
The "fivefold" or "full" gospel structures the narrative of salvation.
Pentecost’s many tongues legitimate many contextual voices (Yong).
positions/pentecostal-theology/keyTexts/: Yong, The Spirit Poured Out on All Flesh (2005)
positions/pentecostal-theology/origin: Pentecostals were long suspicious of academic theology, but from the founding of the Society for Pentecostal Studies (1970) and the Journal of Pentecostal Theology (1992) a scholarly tradition emerged: Walter Hollenweger, Steven Land, Frank Macchia, Simon Chan, Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Amos Yong, Opoku Onyinah.
positions/pentecostal-theology/strongest: It reflects the faith of the fastest-growing Christian movement of the 20th century.
It recovers the Spirit and lived experience neglected by Western theology.
It is global and grassroots, voiced largely from the Global South.
Critics say experience can override Scripture and that excesses (prosperity teaching) lack theological checks.
Cessationists reject its premise that miraculous gifts continue.
Some Pentecostals fear academic theology will domesticate the movement.
positions/pentecostal-theology/responses: Pentecostal scholars themselves criticise prosperity teaching and argue that experience is tested by Scripture and community.
positions/pentecostal-theology/consequen: Ecumenical dialogues with Catholics and Reformed churches.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/oneLine: God is one person; Jesus was a man uniquely empowered (dynamis) by God's Spirit or Word, and in that sense adopted as Son.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/coreClai: The ‘monarchy’ (single rule) of God admits no second divine person.
Jesus was a real human being, born of the Virgin, upon whom the divine power or Word came (often at baptism).
Jesus' divinity is a matter of moral union and divine indwelling, not of nature.
The Word (Logos) is an impersonal attribute or power of God, not a distinct hypostasis.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/origin: Theodotus the Cobbler, a leather-merchant from Byzantium, taught it at Rome c. 190 and was excommunicated by Bishop Victor; Theodotus the Banker and Artemon continued it. Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, gave it its best-known form and was deposed by a synod in 268.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/proponen: Photinus of Sirmium (4th c., similar views)
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/stronges: It preserves strict biblical monotheism without philosophical distinctions of essence and person.
Early sermons in Acts speak of Jesus as ‘a man approved of God’ whom God ‘made… both Lord and Christ’ — language that sounds like exaltation rather than pre-existence.
It takes Jesus' full humanity, growth, prayer and temptation with complete seriousness.
Its adherents claimed it was the original Roman teaching before Bishop Zephyrinus (per Eusebius, HE 5.28).
It cannot account for texts of pre-existence and creation through the Son (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; Philippians 2:6).
It makes the worship of Jesus — already present in the New Testament and in Pliny's report (c. 112) — a worship of a creature.
Salvation as union with God requires that God himself, not a God-inspired man, enter human life (Irenaeus, Athanasius).
The Roman church's own leaders rejected the claim that it was original teaching, and it lost every synod it faced.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/response: Adherents read pre-existence texts as God's plan or Wisdom existing ideally before Christ's birth, not as a personal pre-existence.
They argued that the honour paid to Jesus is honour to the God who exalted him (Philippians 2:9–11).
Later Unitarians and some modern biblical scholars revived the argument that ‘high Christology’ developed after the earliest preaching.
positions/dynamic-monarchianism/conseque: The deposition of Paul of Samosata (268) was an early episcopal judgement on a doctrinal question; when Paul refused to vacate the church building, Christians appealed to Emperor Aurelian.
Its rejection pushed mainstream theology towards Logos theology and, eventually, Nicaea.
Its themes re-emerged in Socinianism, Unitarianism and some liberal Christologies.
positions/modalism/oneLine: There is one God who reveals himself in successive modes or roles — as Father in creation and law, as Son in redemption, as Spirit in sanctification.
positions/modalism/coreClaims/0: God is a single person (prosopon) with three names or modes of activity.
positions/modalism/coreClaims/1: Jesus is fully God, because he is the one God himself incarnate.
positions/modalism/coreClaims/2: ‘Father’ and ‘Son’ describe God in different relations or at different times, not eternally distinct persons.
positions/modalism/coreClaims/3: (In some forms) the Father himself suffered in the incarnate Son — hence the opponents' label ‘Patripassian’.
positions/modalism/origin: Taught at Rome c. 190–215 by Noetus of Smyrna and Praxeas, and systematised by Sabellius (fl. c. 215), who was excommunicated by Pope Callistus. Combated by Hippolytus (Against Noetus) and Tertullian (Against Praxeas).
positions/modalism/proponentsOther/2: Marcellus of Ancyra (accused of similar views, 4th c.)
positions/modalism/strongestArguments/0: It affirms both strict monotheism and the full deity of Christ, which many ordinary believers held together without technical vocabulary.
positions/modalism/strongestArguments/1: Jesus says ‘he that hath seen me hath seen the Father’ (John 14:9) and is called ‘the everlasting Father’ (Isaiah 9:6).
positions/modalism/strongestArguments/2: It avoids what modalists saw as the ‘two gods’ (ditheism) of Logos theologians.
positions/modalism/strongestArguments/3: It made it plain that the God of the Old Testament himself — not a lesser being — came to save.
positions/modalism/strongestObjections/0: The Gospels show the Son praying to the Father, being sent by him, and the Spirit descending at the baptism — real I–Thou relations (Matthew 3:16–17; John 17).
positions/modalism/strongestObjections/1: If the Father became the Son, the Son's revelation of the Father is a revelation of no one beyond himself, and the Son's obedience becomes play-acting.
positions/modalism/strongestObjections/2: ‘Patripassianism’ attributes suffering to the Father in a way most early theologians thought unworthy of God.
positions/modalism/strongestObjections/3: Tertullian: it ‘put to flight the Paraclete, and crucified the Father’.
positions/modalism/responses/0: Modalists answered that prayer and sending reflect the incarnate humanity relating to the divine, not two divine persons.
positions/modalism/responses/1: Later Oneness Pentecostals argue the distinctions are between God's deity and Christ's humanity, not between eternal persons, and that ‘person’ is post-biblical vocabulary.
positions/modalism/responses/2: Some modern theologians (e.g. Barth's ‘modes of being’) have been accused of modalism while denying it, showing the line is subtle.
positions/modalism/consequences/0: Provoked Tertullian's formula ‘one substance, three persons’ and Hippolytus' polemic.
positions/modalism/consequences/1: ‘Sabellian’ became the standard Eastern charge against homoousios in the fourth century, slowing acceptance of Nicaea.
positions/modalism/consequences/2: Revived in the 20th century in Oneness Pentecostalism.
